description.narrative:
Nigeria's economy, ranked 27th globally, is on the cusp of significant transformation due to global economic trends and climate change. The country's heavy reliance on oil exports, accounting for approximately 90% of its foreign exchange earnings, makes it vulnerable to fluctuations in global oil prices (OPEC, 2023). With oil prices projected to decline by 20-30% by 2030 due to the transitionto renewable energy (IEA, 2022), Nigeria's economic stability is under threat. The volatility in oil prices can have far-reaching consequences for Nigeria's economy. Decreased government revenue, reduced investment, high debt rate and increased inflation are potential risks. In 2024, Nigeria's oil revenue declined by 45% due to the market volatility, resulting in a 6.1% contraction in GDP (National Bureau of Statistics, 2024). Furthermore, the country's inflation rate, already high at 32.71% (National Bureau of Statistics, 2024) and may escalate due to reduced government revenue and increased production costs. Political Economy landscape: Important reform decisions have been taken for Nigeria to avoid a fiscal cliff, and temporary compensation is being provided to help the poorestand most vulnerable households. In May and June 2023, the incoming administration undertook two critical policy decisions, which have resulted in price and exchange rate adjustments in the second half of the year. On foreign exchange (FX) policy, progress has been made on implementing the policy for a unified, transparent, and flexible exchange rate. On fiscal policy, budget planning for the next several years is consistent with sustaining the fiscal savings from the subsidy reform and mobilizing more revenues. Inflation remains at record high levels for Nigeria. However, the reforms are yet to be completed to fully realize the economic benefits. The near-term priority is to enhance the reform effort with a closely coordinated mix of fiscal, monetary, and FX policies to reduce inflation and achieve macroeconomic stabilization. The economic outlook for Nigeria in the short to medium term hinges on the continuation and effectiveness of its macroeconomic stabilization agenda. With implementation of these first macroeconomic stabilization reforms, the economy is expected to grow at an averageannual rate of 3.5% during 2023–2026. Climate Change is having a significant impact on Nigeria, affecting various aspects of life, including health, economy, and overall well-being. Nigeria life expectancy has declined over the years and climate-relatedhealth issues contribute to this disparity. Nigeria is particularly vulnerable to climate-related conflicts due to its geographic location where climate change is projected to exacerbate droughts, floods, and heatwaves. Also, pollution from oil extractionand agricultural activities fuels tensions. Climate-related displacement is straining resources and sparking conflicts bringing a new reality as climate immigrants. Nigeria's economy relies heavily on oil and agriculture, making it susceptible to climate-related disruptions. In 2021, Nigeria’s Energy Transition Plan (ETP) was created with COP26 support, promptingNigeria’s net-zero commitment by 2060. The plan maps a pathway to reduce Nigeria’s dependence on fossil fuels, emphasizing renewable energy. However, Nigeria's energy access remains a significant challenge, with a large portion of the population lacking reliable electricity. According to recent data, around 85 million Nigerians lack access to electricity, and many more experience unreliable power. The National Energy Transition Plan (NETP) aims to address this by decarbonizing the energy sector, focusing on renewable energy, and promoting energy efficiency. This aligns with Nigeria's economic diversification goals by reducing dependence on fossilfuels, creating green jobs, and boosting sustainable development. For this to happen legally, there is a need for policy and regulatory change mainly aimed at creating a conducive environment for businesses to invest in energy transition and significantcapacity building and skill development to support roll out and growth of new technologies.
Rising Conflict: Nigeria has over 250 ethnic groups andmultiple religious affiliations, creating potential tensions and prolonged conflicts, including Boko Haram insurgency, Niger Delta militancy, and farmers/herders and communal clashes for scarce resource control and kidnappings for economic gains. Nigeria’s security situation is complex, marked by the involvement of different state and non-state actors in conflicts and human rights violations.While criminality is reported as the primary source of violence, several major conflict drivers include attacks by Islamist groups,counter-insurgency operations, criminal and cult-related violence, separatist movements, and clashes between farmers and herders. Banditry and kidnappings also contributed to the country’s instability. Rising unemployment and High poverty rate, with over 40% of the population living below the poverty line. The removal of fuel subsidyinNigeria has led to a rise in inflation rate. The consumerprice index (CPI) rose to 22.41% in May 2023, up from 22.22% in the previous month, which was the fifth consecutive rise in the country's inflation rate in 2024. The inflation rate increased to32.72%in September 2023, which was a 0.92 percentage point increase from 25.80% recorded in August and as of March 2024, has risen to all time high of 33% there by exacerbating inequality and especiallyincome and social disparities, with a small elite holdinga disproportionate amount of wealth and power. High levels of unemployment, particularly among young people, contribute to social unrest and instability. The unemployment rate in Nigeria was 5% in the thirdquarter of 2023, up from 4.2% in the previous period. The jobless rate among young people aged 15-24 rose to 8.6% from 7.2%. Budgetary Allocation: A breakdown of the 2024 budgetary expenditure estimates showed that the Defence and security sector has the largest share of the total (12%), followedby Education (7.9%), Health (5%), Infrastructure (5%), and Social Investment (2%). This is a far cry from the allocations to the Health and Education sectors following the global benchmarks of 15% (2001 Abuja Declaration) and 15- 20% (UNESCO standards), respectively. Shrinking Civic Space: The Tinubu administration, which took office on May 29, 2023, has been marked by a troubling pattern of neglect towards the concerns and aspirations of large segments of the Nigerian population. This administration appears to be following a path similar to that of its predecessor, the Buhari administration, which was widely criticized for its failure to safeguard the civic space and uphold democratic principles. The current government seems intent on not only maintaining but potentially exacerbating the shortcomings of the Buhari regime, raising serious concerns about the state of democracy and human rights in Nigeria. Perpetrators of violence and censorship often enjoy impunity, perpetuating a culture of fear and silencing dissenting voices. The projections for 2025/2026 are not significantly different from this analysis considering the trend. Local Seed System the Seed Entrepreneurs Association of Nigeria (SEEDAN) serves as the country's seed trade association, with 72 seed companies registered as members in 2019. However, despite the infrastructure and economies of scale of various stakeholders in the seed sector, farmers' access to and utilisation of quality seeds of new and improved varieties still need tobe improved. This limitation contributes to low crop productivity in Nigeria. Seed programming is being negatively impacted in Nigeria due to lack of clear policy and regulation around free seed distribution for farmers. OXFAM in Nigeria and partners are making effort through the Crop Diversity for Food Security Project in West Africa to strengthen local seed system there by enhancing small holder farmer’s capacity to produce and disseminate seeds of new and diverse varieties that are adaptable to localgrowing conditions. The aim is to generate evidence for influencing humanitarian actors to transit from free seed distribution to more sustainable approach of local seed production in order to reduce over dependency of small holder farmers on external support especially in conflict affected communities. However, the national agricultural seed council of Nigeria as the apex seed regulatory body do not currently have a coordination mechanismon how free seed distribution should be conducted in an emergencycontext. Environment <(>&<)> Soil Degradation: Nigeria's civil society has launched a campaign against multinational companies’ divestment believing that the oil companies cannot simply leave the communities they have harmed environmentally and in terms of human rights,without addressing the issues. They also believe that oil companies are divesting because it provides them with an opportunity to abdicate their years of responsibility for the ecological damage in the Niger Delta region. Across project intervening locations in North-West <(>&<)> East it is evident that soil degradation and fertility are two major set -back in achieving food and Nutrition security looking at the heavy reliance of farmers on both organic and in-organic manure as well as prevalence of striga inmost farms. These two are actually counter investment on improving agrarian livelihoods of the poor and vulnerable population in the region. Cultural Values, Belief and Gender Gaps: In most communities across Nigeria women have restrictions on participation level in activities/programs that will improve their lives and livelihood and place them in a better position to make meaningful contributions to the societies. it is becoming more prevalent to have women participate by proxy in northern Nigeria especially the North-West for instance in Gumel LGA of Jigawa State where currently we have farmerfield school (FFS) program on crop variety testing and seed multiplication only 1 FFS have 5 women out of the 5 FFS of 30 participants each, while inthe neighbouring LGA each of the 5 FFS have only 5 women with 25 men. This highlights the need to close the gendergap in education and the rising need to prioritize girl-child education. According to UNICEF,7.6 million girls are out of school (OOS) in Nigeria;3.9 million at the primary and 3.7 million at the junior secondary level. More than 50% of girls are not attending school at the basic education level, 48% of OOS girls are in the North-west and North-east. Opportunities: Food security in crisis: Nigeria has abundant agricultural resources that can ensure national food security, yet food insecurity persists, due to several challenges. Unfortunately, while Nigeria, is still grappling with these multiple problems driving food insecurity, the Russia-Ukraine crisis has brought a new dimension to food insecurity. Nigeria’s dependence on importation from Russia and Ukraine, particularly for maize and wheat, contributes to increased prices of maize and wheat products, in the face of increasing inflation in the country. While the Russia-Ukraine crisis has led to food shortages in countries that depend on them for raw and finished agricultural produce/products, the situation also throws up opportunities for countries, especially countries like Nigeria with vastopportunities for ensuring food security. Nigeria's youth population is estimated to be around 160 million, or 70% of the country's population. Nigeria has one of the youngest populations in the world, with a median age of 17.9 years. This youthful demographyprovides a large, affordable labour force that can drive mass production of cash crops in high demand globally such as cocoa, oil palm and cashew. Nigeria’s agricultural sector is brimming with untapped potential presenting vast opportunities. This, alongside the youth demographic does lay a groundwork for innovative agricultural practices and agribusiness entrepreneurship in alignment with Oxfam in Nigeria Country Strategic Plan and Oxfam Global Strategic Framework of those we would be working with for impact. Digital economy: the government multi-pronged digital transformative efforts launched such as the 3 Million Technical Talent (3MTT) Programme and the Broadband Alliance provides opportunities for youth participation and digital economy growth across sectors. These initiatives aim to improve productivityacross sectors through technology and presents opportunities to equip young people with the skills and knowledge needed to drive innovation as a foundation for growing the digital economy. This provides opportunities for advancing impact of digital technologies on equality, gender, social well-being and civic space. Local Government Autonomy: within the governance structure, the local government remains the closest link between the government andits citizens. However, their effectiveness hinges significantly on one crucial factor: financial autonomy. The Supreme court in its judgement 2024 decided that the LGAs can now directly receive their allocations from the federation account.Effective and efficient function of the local government will address inequality and prioritise on people’s power by ensuring basic social services are available for the most vulnerable. Economic Diversification: Nigeria must diversify its economy, investing in non-oil sectors like manufacturing, services, and renewable energy. The manufacturing sector, currentlyaccounting for 10% of GDP, has the potential to contribute 20% by 2030 (Manufacturers Association of Nigeria, 2022). The country’s renewable energy sector can create 100,000 jobs and attract $10 billion in investments by 2050 (International Renewable Energy Agency, 2022). Tax Reforms: Nigeria’s tax system has long been riddled with gross inefficiencies, leakages, structural imbalances, and a glaring lack of equity in income distribution and the tax burden. However, recent reforms advocated by the Presidential Tax Reform Committee is pushing for a more transformative and progressive tax system for improved equity and equality. The provisions toeliminatetaxes for low-income earners disproportionately saddled with tax burdens will foster equity in the tax system and correct some systemic anomalies. Poor people are forced to pay official and unofficial taxes. Ordinary, workers are subjected to PAYE taxes that are often not remitted by employers to tax authorities. Unofficial taxes paid to non-state actors extracted from transport fares paid bylow-income earners to transport sector unions in Lagos alone were estimated at N200 billion a year. The tax reforms, which are significant and comprehensive, can elevate taxation as the key revenue earner for the government and correct the distortions created by Nigeria’s oil-dependent rentier economy that has failed to foster equitable distribution of resources and hobbled socioeconomic development for decades. This further provides the opportunity for Oxfam in Nigeria to engage with the Ministry of Budget and Economic Planning, other government Ministries Departments Agencies (MDAs) and relevant policymakers to influence these reforms riding on the recently launched Oxfam inequality report in Nigeria. 1.2 Internal Context Internal changes within Oxfam in Nigeria, such as new policies or structural adjustments, have a significant impact on organizational work and operations by reshaping how resources, personnel, and strategic priorities are managed. This informed the collaboration between Oxfam Ghana, Nigeria, and Senegal to develop a strategy for engagement with ECOWAS 2024 to 2028 which is focused and in alignment with Oxfam’s regional focus and the ECOWAS Human Capital Development Plan 2030. This strategy document will guide Oxfam in Ghana, Nigeria and Senegal alongside identified strategic partners to inform priority areas of engagement with ECOWAS and other regional platforms for influencing and campaigns. Section 2: Horizon 2 Roadmap – Lenses Oxfam will continue to focus on addressing inequality by dismantling patriarchal structures, amplification of marginalised voices, promoting civic participation and platforms, improve inclusive socio-political participation by embedding the lenses across all levels of programming to serve the diverse needs and experiences of different groups. This will be achieved by focusing on the following: • Inequalities Lens Oxfam's campaigns on inequality perfectly align with the programmes' goal of ensuring socio-economic and politicalrights for Nigerians,working together with citizens, institutions, and the private sector, with the aims to promote transparency and accountability, essential for transforming Nigeria's extractive sector earnings, promoting fair taxation, participatory budget into improved living standards and an inclusive governance process for its citizens. Nigeria, now Africa’s 4th largest economy falling from its first place in the last one year, faces extreme levels of inequality, with over 130 million people living in poverty. The richest Nigerian man'sannual wealth earnings could lif11t 2 million people out of poverty for a year. This staggering disparity underscores the need for policy reforms and accountable governance. The recent #EndBadGovernance protests, the #EndSARS movement, and Nigeria Labour Congressdemonstrations highlight the urgent need for public social accountability and democratic empowerment in Nigeria. Economic literacy and advocacy are crucial in addressing the country's economichardships, which have led to widespread discontent among citizens. If the programme is able to programme around promoting participatory budgeting and tracking, fair taxation, and inequality, remediation in the extractives industry, the teamcan ensure that Nigeria’s natural resources benefit everyone, not just a privileged few. This can be addressed through targeting policy reforms, such as engaging the presidential committee on tax and fiscal reforms, promoting the implementation of the petroleum industry law and engaging the financial sector in the fight against illicit financial flows at all levels of governance. Civic education, election and leadership empowerment are also vital in promoting democracy and good governance. This includesempowering citizens with theknowledge and skills to participate in decision-making processes, holding leaders accountable, and promoting transparency and accountability. The #EndBadGovernance protests, which began on August 1, 2024, demonstrate the power of citizen mobilization in demanding change. However, the government's response, including the use of force and arrests, underscores the need for sustained advocacy and education to ensure that citizens' rights are respected and protected. By supportingdemocratic empowerment and public social accountability initiatives, Nigerians can build a more just and equitable society. Prioritizing our campaign against inequality through these components, the programme is able to ensure citizen participation in good governanceand promoting transparency and accountability is vital for Nigeria's democratic growth. This can be achieved through initiatives that strengthen civic education, enhance access to information, and support participatory budgeting. Empoweringcitizens to hold leaders accountable through advocacy and activism can also foster a culture of transparency. Furthermore, supporting independent media andanti-corruption agencies can help expose and address corruption and promote citizen engagement andaccountability, while building trust in institutions and ensuring that government policies and programmes serve the needs of all Nigerians. • Civic Space Lens Protecting and expanding civic space in Nigeria is crucial for promoting democratic governance, human rights, and sustainabledevelopment. Unfortunately, Nigeria's civic space has been shrinking dramatically due to various factors, including declining democratic values, conflict, and political instability. The country has witnessed a vicious crackdown on social critics, bloggers, and activists challenging impunity, official corruption, and human rights abuses since 2015. Some of the factors contributing to Shrinking Civic Space include restrictive legislation, such as the NGO Regulatory Bill, which aims to regulatethe activities of non-governmental organizations even though has been suppressed over the years by civil society, the bill has continued to resurface after the inauguration of every parliament since its inception in 2010 and the enactment of the Company Income and Allied Matters Act. Additionally, the misuseof emergency laws, consolidation of government power, and the influence of private interests have also played a significant role inlimiting civic engagement. The growing restrictions on free speech,association, and assembly rights have created a climate of fear,making it challenging for citizens and civil society organizations to operate freely. Despite these challenges, Oxfam, partners together with various actors, informal groups, and organizedcivil society, are working tirelessly to reclaim civic space and demand greater respect for human rights and fundamental freedoms. Some of the strategies we have imbibed and will continue to deploy to reclaim civic space include advocating for non-violent solutions to civil conflict, publicly condemning brutal arrests and excessive force, and forging alliances with other civic society groups. Leveraging digital technologies, particularly social media, has also been effective in facilitating meaningful engagement, activism, and mobilization. • Decolonial Feminist Approaches Lens This is done by situating approaches within the specific context by recognising progressive indigenous practices and building on or strengthening existing structures and knowledge that embrace fairness and diversified development approaches. Oxfam in Nigeria adopts approaches that challenges and promote feminist principles through the various program intervention, the gender standalone project exemplifies a decolonial feminist approach by actively challenging entrenched power structures and fostering equitable and transformative practices. The project aligns this lens by addressing structural inequalities, it acknowledges historical and systemic barriers to women’s empowerment,tailoring solutions to local realities reducing inequality through Equity. Oxfam uses community-driven approaches to promoteequality and ensure that marginalized voices—especially women’s—are amplified, not sidelined, in decision-making processes. One of the approachesis promoting Positive Masculinity through the gender transformative approaches training i.e. RCA, GALs and transformative leadership for women’s rights. The Involvement of men and boys in discussions on positive masculinity fosters shared responsibility for societal transformation as gender champions, adopting peer to peer participation with men leading some of the dialogues session and mainstreaming gender in all Oxfam programming.
One of the approaches OiN adopts to challenge power structure and promote feminist principles, is to facilitate the design and development of the National Workplace Gender Policy in partnership with relevant ministries (Ministry of Women Affairs and Ministry of Labour). The policy aims to reduce disparities between women and men in accessto, control over and benefit from economic, social, educational and career development resources, opportunities, and services, suchas equal pay for work of equal value. , Creating a harmonious work-life balance for bothwomen and men; and equal representation ofwomen in business and management roles, and Investment in a future of work that works for women. . A draft policy was development with Oxfam’s support and has been validated. This is currentlyawaiting accent by the Federal Executive Council for it to be become a national document. Sensitization across relevant stakeholders has been done to enable awareness and facilitate a call to action by the Federal Executive Council. OiN will align with the global frameworkto integrate Decolonial Feminist Approaches across its team and programming in line with GSF commitments and Horizon 2 Roadmap in 2025 that a critical analysis of power and promotes collective transformation of OiN, its partners and across the different focus areas of our work towards ensuring a more equal, just and decolonial futures.

However, this is a piece of work which would bestbe done under the Humanitarian Programme is the programme has capacity. OiN would respond to crises through a multifaceted approach that includes immediate relief, peace building among conflicting entities in a preventive and mitigative approaches as was implemented in the anticipatory action electoral response project funded by STARTFUND,like scarce resource management between communities and herders, campaigns for prevention of electoral violence before general elections in flashpoint locations with short term and long-term development strategies. In emergencies, OiN provide essential servicessuch as WASH, NFI and cash vouchers while advocating for vulnerable populations and coordinating with other humanitarian actors. OiN focus extends beyond immediate needs to include disaster preparedness, early warning, resilience building, and livelihood recovery. OiN emphasizes gender equality, environmental sustainability, and community empowerment, ensuring that affected populations play an active role in rebuilding. Through monitoring, learning, and accountability, OiN ensures its interventions lead to lasting improvements, fostering local leadership and reducing dependence on international aid. Long-Term Development and Sustainable Increased Livelihoods Food Security and Livelihoods: We support smallholder farmers by improving their access to resources, finance (including microcredit), and building the capacity of local businesses and farmers to increase productivity and income and advocating for policiesthat promote sustainable agriculture. Economic Empowerment: Oxfam Nigeria is dedicated to advancing women's economic empowerment byaddressing the barriers that limit their access to opportunities, such as land, credit, and decision-making power. We support women’s groups and cooperatives by organizing them into small savings groups that provide capital for small businesses. Additionally, we offer training in skills development, entrepreneurship, and leadership, while also providing access to better seeds, tools, and markets to enhance productivity. We also run programs that equip young people with the skills needed for the future economy, including vocational training, digital literacy, and entrepreneurship development. Oxfam Nigeria advocates forgovernment policies that create aconducive environment for economic empowerment, environmental protection and rights, focusing on areas such as tax reforms, social protection, and anti-corruption efforts, climate justice and gender justice. We also workto strengthen the capacity of civil societyorganizations to hold the government accountable for economic issues and ensure the equitable distribution of resources. Advocacy and Policy Change: We work to influencepolicies and practices that address the root causes of poverty and inequality, and policies like the Right to food, Climate change Act, that create better opportunities for small-scale producers, and push for more equitable economic systems that address poverty and inequality such as gender-responsive budgeting and fair trade and taxation. We are ensuring Long-Term Impact by: Community-Led Approaches: Oxfam empowers communities to take ownership of their development and participate in decision-making processes. Building Partnerships: We collaborate with local organizations, government agencies, and other stakeholders to strengthen our impact and ensure sustainability. Utilizing technology, such as knowledge and evidence databases, streamlines knowledge sharing and data analysis, enabling better decision-making and impact measurement. The challenges faced by OiN in managing knowledge exchange and collaboration comes largely from the gaps in communication and coordination among multiple stakeholders, including affiliates, donors, local experts, and community members. These gaps can affect the timely sharing of important knowledge and the seamless implementation of programs, affecting the effectiveness of interventions and leading to missed opportunities for learning and improvement. OiN works with diverse set of stakeholders who often have different priorities, timeframes, and communication systems, which can result in silos and fragmented information flows. To address these challenges, OiN will focus on establishing regular, structured knowledge-sharing sessions among all stakeholders. These sessions will serve as a platform for exchanging experiences,discussing best practices, and addressing emerging issues, ensuring that valuable insights are shared in a timely and effective manner. By institutionalizing these sessions, OiN aims to foster a culture of continuous learning and collaboration, breaking down communication barriers and ensuring that all voices are heard. Another key strategy OiN will use to overcome these challenges is the prioritization of capacity-building at the local level. By strengthening the ability of local partners and community stakeholders to generate, use, and share knowledge, OiN can enhance the relevance and applicability of its interventions as local actorsoften have a deeper understanding of the specific challenges and opportunities within their communities, and empowering them with the tools and skills to document and share knowledge ensures that solutions are contextually appropriate and sustainable. Embracing technology is another essential element in addressing coordination challenges, by leveraging digital platforms such as the knowledge and evidence database for collaboration, data collection, and knowledge sharing, OiN can streamline processes, facilitate real-time communication,and ensure thatkey information is easily accessible. This can support remote collaboration, making it easier for geographically dispersed teams to stay connected, share updates, and collaborate on decision-making, thus improving overall program efficiency and impact. OiN’s knowledge and learning practices are closely linked to our existing MEAL processes like the CAMSA, ensuring that the evidence we generate answers key learning questions and feeds into ongoing programmatic improvements. The data collected through ourMEALframeworks will be used to inform and answer our learning questions, providing evidence on the effectiveness, impact, and relevanceof our interventions. Regular monitoring and evaluation activities will help ensure that the learning questions remain aligned withthe project’s/program goals, while also enabling adaptive learning as the project and programs progresses. In terms of contributingto Oxfam's knowledge and evidence database, we plan to systematically collect, and update material related to our learning questions, including reports, case studies, and evaluations etc. on the database on a quarterly basis. Team members assigned to be contributors on the database will participate in training onhow to upload content and make use of the database; they will also ensure that all available materials to be uploaded are collected from different projects and programs within the quarter and uploaded. This effortwill strengthen our contribution to Oxfam’s broader knowledge-sharing objectives, ensuring that lessons learned are captured and available for future programming.
4.3 Influencing To drive systemic change, Oxfam Nigeria incorporates influencing strategies by first conducting a thorough contextual analysis and power mapping to understand the socio-political landscape and identify key stakeholders at national and sub-national. Clear objectives are set, focusing on policy changes and systemic reforms that align with Oxfam’s mission. Partnerships are formed with civil society organizations, community leaders, and other stakeholders to build coalitions andamplify marginalized voices. An evidence-based advocacy that plays a critical role, using data, research, and real-life stories to highlight systemic issues and propose solutions. Public campaigns, both online and offline, are used to raise awareness and mobilizesupport, while facilitate policy engagement that involves facilitating dialogues and lobbying policymakers. Oxfam Nigeria also invests in capacity building, empowering local actors and training advocates to strengthen their advocacy skills. Leveraging global networks and partnerships, Oxfam Nigeria amplifies local issues on international platforms and coordinates with regional campaigns to broaden the impact. Continuous monitoring and feedback ensure strategies remain effective, with lessons learned documented for future initiatives. Oxfam in Nigeria will prioritize on research in partnership with academic institutions on pertinent areas to inform influencing and policy reforms. Through this, it will inform available resourcesfor donor engagement and fundraising. 4.4 Digital Rights and Space: Oxfam in Nigeria (OiN) strategically leverages digital technology to enhance its operations and advocacy efforts while ensuring the rights and well-being of its stakeholders. Through tools like mobile surveys and geospatial mapping, OiN collects real-time data to inform decision-making and optimize resource allocation. Furthermore, social media platforms and webinars amplify advocacy, foster engagement, and expand the reach of OiN's programs. To ensure these interventions are both impactful and ethical, OiN prioritizes robust measures to mitigate digital risks. Data encryption, regular security audits, and staff training are key componentsof OiN’s cybersecurity strategy. Beneficiary data is safeguarded through anonymization and transparent consent processes, while continuous risk assessments and scenario planning help prepare for potentialdigital disruptions. OiN also bridges the digitaldivide by ensuring vulnerable populations can access digital tools and providing low-tech alternatives when necessary. In alignment with its overarching strategy, OiN is enhancing its digital presence through initiatives like targeted email campaigns, newsletters, and online petitions to mobilize support. OiN’s approach to digital technology is rooted in ethical standards and inclusivity. The "do no harm" principle guides the design and execution of digital solutions, with meticulous impact assessments to minimize potential harm, particularly to vulnerable groups. By actively engaging communities, especially women, girls, and marginalized groups, OiN ensures that digital solutions are inclusive, representative, and context specific. Acknowledging gender disparities in digital access, OiN is committed to bridging the digital gender gap by providing equal opportunities for women and girls to benefit from and contribute to technological interventions. Thiswould be explored through available funding opportunities and build on the “Work in Progress (WiP)project in collaboration with suitable partners. Ongoing digital literacy programs empower community members to navigate and benefit from digital technologies safely, fostering an inclusive and equitable digital landscape. Collaboration with local and internationalpartners enables OiN to address common digital rights challenges, share best practices, and maximize impact. Additionally, OiN has enrolled inthe Federal Government of Nigeria's data rights database to uphold accountability and privacy. Thisensures that all technological initiatives align with national data protection standards, safeguarding the privacy and dignity of the people OiN serves. 4.5 Transformative Partnerships To ensure Oxfam in Nigeria are working toward meaningful, long-lasting change, OiN will engage where feasible in a range of relationships with different actors and allies with a shared vision and values to help meet planned goals. This will mean identifying where our objectives overlap and how we can leverage each other’s strengths to achieve a collective impact.These relationships will be based on OiN's partnership principles of shared values and vision; complementarity;autonomy and independence; transparency and mutual accountability; clarity on responsibilities and commitment to joint learning. OiN will ensure Oxfam principles are promoted and implemented by bringing together different actors to work on common problems. OiN will also establish values such as trust and open communication to create a strong partnershipwhile fostering an environment where all partners feel empowered to contribute and share ideas.
Over the years, OiN has largely implemented its programmes through partners while providing themwith technical and organisational capacity strengthening to improve program quality. The country program will continue to adopt approaches that will promote collaboration, shared learning, and risk management among the partners OiN will work with. Oxfam will continue build on its current experience and tools such as ‘Participate in partner Risk Management’ (PRISMA) and other capacity assessment tools available with partners to identify areas where improvement is needed to strengthen partners organizational and technical capacities while strategically allocating resources to build strong, transformative partnerships over the next year. These investments will foster collaboration, empower local partners, and contribute to positive change in the communities served by Oxfam. Specific areas of investment will be capacity building and training, strategic Planning and prioritization, collaborative program design, resource mobilization, inclusive governance structures, monitoring and evaluation frameworks, knowledge sharing platforms, community engagement initiatives, diversity and inclusion initiatives, increasing percentage of funding channelized through local partners, and prioritizing a fair distribution of funds that reflects the contributions and needs of local partners.
Through Program Quality Review meetings,learning reviews and feedback OiN will continue to engage partners and ensure knowledge sharing. OiN will also work withpartners to hold duty-bearers toaccount for recognizing, protecting and fulfilling the rights of women and men living with poverty and injustice. Oxfam will also promote and facilitate meaningful and objective dialogue between the National and Local CSOs and the international agencies to create mutual understanding and trust needed for transformational partnerships. Together with partners, OiN will create opportunities for communities to participate at all levels of project. By sensitizing partners on Oxfam’s partnership principles and Horizon 2 Roadmap towards ensuring a more collaborative and inclusive support across areas of focus and commitments especially on global, regional or national campaigns and application of the four lenses (inequalities, civic spaces, decolonial feminist approaches and rights, resilience and response) acrossour programming and framework agreements.
Section 5: Business Operations 5.1 People Managing staff recruitment, retention, and well-being at Oxfam in Nigeria requires a holistic approach to attract, support, and engage talented individuals, fostering sustained commitment to the organization’s mission. Key strategies include: • Recruitment: Oxfam in Nigeria focuses its recruitment on donor-funded projects mostly in Adamawa and Borno states where new funding has been secured, aiming to attract candidates whose skills and values align with Oxfam’smission. Recruitment strategies include partnerships with networks such as the INGO Forum Group, social media platform for wider reach, and well-defined job descriptions. The global HR platform, SuccessFactors, streamlines recruitment, enabling consistent application of recruitment policies and efficient management across national and global job sites, including Oxfam’s career site. • Retention: Oxfam in Nigeria supports retention through a strong emphasis on career growth, including capacity-building opportunities and internal promotions to encourage career progression. Retention efforts also include competitive compensation packages, with regular salary adjustments on an annual basis, and reviews onallowances as it relates to the high rise of Inflation and Economic Situation. Feedback and engagement assessments are conducted regularly to ensure a fulfilling and supportive workplace. • Well-being: Oxfam in Nigeria prioritizes staff well-being through comprehensive health and insurance benefits, pension plans, flexible working arrangements, end-of-year review meetings/staff retreats, and team-building activities. Work-life balance is a core element of Oxfam’s approach, recognizing that a healthy, balanced staff is essential to organizational success. Through these strategies, Oxfam in Nigeria aims to cultivate a skilled, motivated, and resilient team, capable of thriving and contributing to the organization’s mission over the long term. 5.2 Safeguarding Oxfam in Nigeria alignsits activities with the "Do No Harm" principle, ensuring that our interventions do not cause harm to the communities in which we work. Upon recruitment, all Oxfam in Nigeriastaff undergo a comprehensive induction on safeguarding, which includes completing Oxfam'smandatory safeguarding e-learning course and participating in a 1:1 induction session on safeguarding. Additionally, a risk assessment is conducted on our partnersat the outset of engagement to evaluate their safeguarding risks and determine the most effective ways to support them in addressing these needs. Oxfam in Nigeria supports partner organizations in developing safeguarding policies where none exist and strengthen existing policies to ensure compliance with safeguarding standards. Furthermore, OiN assists partners in identifying safeguarding focal points within their organizations and establishing focal points across all OiN offices. These focal points arethen trained on safeguarding practices in alignment withOxfam’s standards and the United Nations safeguarding principles. The Safeguarding Resource and Support Hub (RSH) serves as a resource center for focal points. Partners also receive training on thedevelopment of Community-Based Feedback and Complaint Mechanisms (CBFMs) to enable the confidential and accessible reporting of safeguarding concerns through context-appropriate channels. Safeguarding sessions are integrated into project activities to sensitize participants about safeguarding principles and ensure that CBFMs are well known and effectively utilized. Complaint channels are developed with community input ensuring inclusivity, particularly addressing the needs of persons with disabilities (PWDs), women, and children. 5.3 Income and Business Development • Identify/generate innovative ideas that respond to prevailing needs of communities especially, the most vulnerable. This will be done through generating case studies, documenting stories of change and lessons learnt to inform innovative project design and donor engagement. • Identify skilled resources that will support the delivery of quality proposals in response to the donor’s calls where the, require expertise is not available within the country team. • Prioritise on strategic opportunities: sorting and prioritising on innovations and calls that are most strategic in terms of funding envelop, areas of footprints and available resource to implement. • Develop possible prototypes to understand the feasibility of the ideas and possibledevelopment of a concept/proposal which addresses any gap/bottleneck. This will build on the case studies, stories of change from the field/implemented projects. • Donor mapping and engagement to betterunderstand donor’s funding priority and focus to inform the proposals (solicited/unsolicited). Regular donormapping and understanding of the political economy landscape to better identify possible donors that align with the country strategic plan and goal areas. • Tasking all programme team with fundraising targets. This will encourage ownership and exploringfurther opportunities across thematic areas for possible positioning. • We will strategically approach likeminded organizations in our sector and forge strong Consortium's to attract long term funding opportunities. • Proactively approach new donors seeking for long term funding and strategic partnerships that will in the long run bring trust to manage bigger and long-term funding.
These are part of the strategies for the country funding plan to strengthen fundraising. Engagements are ongoing with the OiA business development unit especially, in exploring funding opportunities and additional PAs to further improve the funding landscape for the country office. 5.4 Security Oxfam in Nigeria approach to managing security risks in high-risk areas issustained through proactive strategies, collaborative efforts, and continuous adaptation to evolving threats. Our Security Management Plan and detailed security guidelines are the foundation of our efforts,enabling systematic and consistent management of securitychallenges in volatile environments. Key highlights of OiN security risk management are: • Conducting regular security risk assessments to identify emerging risks and vulnerabilities; develop andimplement tailored mitigation measures that includestrict adherence to field movement regulations and advisories, ensuring all movements are planned and authorized under secure protocols. • Prioritizing capacity building by providing security training and awareness sessions such as Hostile Environment Awareness Training (HEAT), Journey Management, First Aid, and Incident Reporting protocols for staff and partners to enhance preparedness and resilience during program implementation. • Fostering strong coordination with security actors, partners, and community stakeholders building trust andenhancing situational awareness and response capacity, by continuously monitoring the security atmospheric and adapting Oxfam strategies to protect staff members, partners, assets, and operations effectively. • Establishing critical incident management framework to enable rapid and effective emergency responses, with clearly defined communication channels, roles, and procedures to enhance preparedness. • Strengthening contingency planning by expanding contingency plans to include responses to shifting operational environments, such as restricted civic spaces or heightened regulatory assessment. Also, incorporates scenarios for mass evacuations, shelter-in-place situations, and prolonged access constraints. • Investing in communication and surveillance tools, such as satellite phones, and GPS trackers to enhance situational awareness and emergency communication. • Implementing digital platforms for real-time security monitoring and reporting.
• Increasing resources for security focal points and coordinators who oversee localized security planning and incident responses. • Developing low-profile operational approaches to minimize visibility and reduce exposureto risk. •OiN collaborates with partners to aid inensuring a unified security posture, by providing technical support in developing partner-specific security risk assessments and plans, facilitate joint training sessions to enhance partners security capabilities, and sharecritical resources, including security intelligence, tools, and access to contingency framework. Additionally, Oxfam assists partners in identifying security focal points within their organizations. These focal points are trained toreport incidents from field locations effectively. •Integrating these approaches into our security risk management strategy, Oxfam in Nigeria aim to mitigate riskseffectively, protect staff, partners, assets, and maintain operational/business continuity in challenging environments (high-risk area) 5.5 Going Green Promoting environmental sustainability means adopting environmentally friendly practices and reducing harmful impacts on the environment as an organisation and as individuals as staff. Actions taken include • Raising awareness: Providing information on environmental issues, climate change, and sustainable practices, activities and programs. • Educating and providing information and statistics on current global trends and best practices on sustainable environmental practices. and resources like reducingcarbon footprint. • Supporting sustainable environmental actions: Providing technical and other support to reputable environmental causes, organizations and initiatives. Advocate and promote environmentally friendly policies. Such as, planting of trees, movement building, climate caravan, annual quiz competition, green challenge. • Fostering community engagement: Facilitating discussions and sharing user-generated content on environmental topics through town hall meetings, women climate dayof action in Niger Delta Week ofAction, setting up climate clubs in schools and colleges, media reporting competition. • Reducing carbon footprint: Optimizing datastorage, transmission, and server efficiency and reducing paper works, using reusable drinking cups, work from home to reduce fossil emission and printing of hard copy materials. • Encouraging eco-friendly habits within and outside Oxfam by raising environmental consciousness: Sharing tips on energy efficiency, waste reduction, and sustainable living. • Implement sustainable supply chain practices through the use eco-friendly packaging and procurement- Buy sustainable, locally sourced products. • Invest in renewable energy by solar inverter and reduction in the number of hours the generator runs. • Reduce water usage/wastage. • Implement recycling programs. • Promote sustainable transportation such as reduction in commuting to the office and commuting as a group to events/activities. • Conduct carbon footprint assessments. • Develop sustainable workforce practices, using e-business cards and QR codes. • Createa green space (e.g., garden, indoor plants). • Upgrade to energy-efficient appliances. • Recycle and compost. • Support renewable energy policies and advocacy.
